blocks.text: (Pause)
(In the presence of the jury)
Good morning. Everything's there? Good.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: My Lord, we'll be looking at evidence that's contained on the second sequence of events for [Baby I]. May I recall Dr Matthew Neame, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR MATTHEW NEAME (continued)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER (continued)

When we broke off on Friday, we were about to consider your involvement with the baby [Baby I] on 13 October onwards, so may I return there, please, and ask Mr Murphy to put on screen tile 49 of the second sequence of events, which you'll see, Dr Neame, refers to notes written by you at 04.45 about events at 03.23 hours on 13 October.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we could go to Dr Neame's notes, please. We'll see that you noted that you responded to a bleep call at 03.23 to attend the neonatal unit. And that, we understand, is this right, Dr Neame, is an urgent call for attention?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I don't recall whether it was a sort of crash bleep or an urgent phone call bleep.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But at the very least it's an urgent invitation for you to attend on a patient?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And on arrival, you could see, could you, nurses providing assistance to baby [Baby I]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And that they were providing care, is this right, with breathing support --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- in the form of Neopuff ventilation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And could you continue and tell us what else you recall and what else you have noted about that event?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I also noted that [Baby I] was receiving chest compressions and that she was pale and floppy at that time.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So did you join in or indeed take over the management of the assistance being given to the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I took over managing [Baby I]'s airway.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: How did you do that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So in my note I've documented that I used something called a double-handed jaw thrust, so that's an alternative method for managing an airway and improving management of the airway.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Is that intended to ensure the airway was patent?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And upon doing so, could you notice any success?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So with that manoeuvre, [Baby I]'s chest wall was noted to be moving with the ventilation breaths. I also increased the pressure on the breathing support to help with the resuscitation. Then I've continued with my assessment.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry to interrupt you, "double-handed jaw thrust", then the next word?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "Initiated."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "Initiated", right. "Chest movement..."?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "... detected and satisfactory."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm not critical, but it's very difficult writing to read.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: In terms of chest movement, the procedure, the intervention, that you initiated was successful. Did it have the desired effect immediately with regard to the baby's heart rate?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At that point, her heart rate was still around 60 beats per minute, so that's lower than normal and lower than we would like.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Did you continue to provide her with urgent assistance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The chest compressions were continued because of that.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: If we scroll up, please:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Therefore CPR continued..."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry, scroll down, I always get that wrong.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Just below the hole punch that we can see on the screen there, did you intubate the baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So the documentation states:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "Intubated due to need for secure airway. Three-millimetre breathing tube [ETT] passed to 8 centimetres at the lips on first attempt and capnography positive..."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So the carbon dioxide test was positive:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "... and there was equal air entry on auscultating."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So listening to [Baby I]'s chest with a stethoscope.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So that was a successful intubation --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- at first attempt? The capnography monitor indicated that she was exhaling carbon dioxide and, when listening, it sounded right --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- on both lungs? Was that the end of the urgent assistance given to [Baby I] or did it continue?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, the cardiac compressions continued in the usual three chest compressions to one breath from the breathing support ratio. I tested [Baby I]'s chest with a cold light to detect any evidence of pneumothorax and in my documentation I've also recorded that I asked for Dr Newby to be contacted as I was placing the ETT breathing tube.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So you summoned, called for the on-call consultant. What was the result of the cold light test, the examination for pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was a negative test showing or demonstrating that there was no evidence of a pneumothorax using that test.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "[Minus sign] VE", negative?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: We know from earlier evidence, I think from yourself, certainly at least from some witnesses, that the cold light test would be the initial immediate test done and later a more
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: thorough examination through an X-ray would almost, by way of routine, be undertaken to double-check --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Newby arrived. We'll hear from Dr Newby in due course, but we know from the times recorded on this presentational document that she arrived at 03.36, that is to say, about 13 minutes after your arrival at [Baby I]'s cot side.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So Dr Newby will pick up the narrative of those events in due course, so we won't go over it twice. Can I move you forward in time, please, to a few hours later and go to tile 95 and the events of 05.20 hours on 13 October.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Tile 95, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but my pad's gone wrong:
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: "App connection status: not connected to courtroom."
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (Pause)

It sounds as though we've got a bit of a problem here. I'm just wondering whether we could continue but everything must be put up on the screen, Mr Driver, that's referred to. Oh, it's come back again. It's come back again now. Mine has.
How many won't log in, could you raise a hand?
(Pause)
In the circumstances, could I ask Mr Murphy to take us back to tile 49 then, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you. And the notes behind.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go to the bottom of this page, please. After the cold light negative, we see that Dr Newby was contacted as the ET tube was being placed:
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "Drugs given as described above..."
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: "... above with ongoing chest compression/CPR until 03.45, as documented in Dr Newby's note."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So we'll refer to Dr Newby's note with Dr Newby. If we could look at the next page, which is beneath, also on this tile, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The time, 05.20; is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Okay. Does that say "currently"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Does that refer to the state of play as of 05.20?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And what was the assistance being given to the baby at that point as documented in your note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby I] was being managed on a ventilator with the settings described as SIMV 22/5, oxygen concentration of 43%, tidal volumes of approximately 5ml per kilogram, equal air entry. [Baby I] was being managed with 150ml per kilogram per day of fluids, which was 10% dextrose; she was no longer being fed. There's a description of a blood transfusion being provided. [Baby I]'s mean arterial pressure, so her measurement of her blood pressure, was 35 to 40 on a cuff blood pressure monitor.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: I have recorded that she was mottled with normal heart sounds and that she had been started on some antibiotics: ciprofloxacin, teicoplanin and metronidazole.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Taking some of those features in turn, the tidal volume, we are led to understand in other evidence, is a measurement of the air going in and out of the lungs?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: That measurement, is that a satisfactory reading or otherwise?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's a satisfactory reading.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Blood pressure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, satisfactory and acceptable for a baby of [Baby I]'s gestation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So looking at it globally, those measurements that you took at 05.20, what sort of picture did they reflect for [Baby I]'s state of health at that snapshot in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: For a baby who's requiring significant respiratory support, she's otherwise stable.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You did refer, when we just had the break for the replacement of the iPads, to tile 95. So that note appears again in tile 95 in the sequence, but it's more convenient to follow it on --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It does indeed. The second page, the page that we are currently looking at --
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The second page that we just looked at, because that's later on in the sequence of events. All right.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: If we could look at the remainder of this page, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there a chest X-ray?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, that's an X-ray note.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Is it your note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, it is.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Your examination of the chest X-ray?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: What did that inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The breathing tube was placed too far in at that point, so it was withdrawn 1 centimetre from 8.5 centimetres to 7.5 centimetres at [Baby I]'s lips.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Pausing there, when you say it was placed too far in, was it much too far in, slightly too far in or what?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it was further in than the optimal position. There's a risk that if it goes further than where it was, it would only be effectively ventilating one lung due to the anatomy. That's the reason to move it.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So that was corrected. Is that the ET tube that you intubated [Baby I] with --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- as per your evidence a few minutes ago?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So that was corrected?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: You then considered the nasogastric tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, which appeared to be curled in [Baby I]'s oesophagus, so essentially not placed far enough in, it hadn't reached her stomach. Then I've documented that I had made the nurse, Lucy Letby, aware and I have recorded that she had agreed to re-pass the tube.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Let's remind ourselves: intubation, is that a procedure always undertaken by medics, by doctors?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In Chester at that time, it would have only been undertaken by a doctor, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But a repositioning of a nasogastric tube could be undertaken by a doctor or a nurse?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Nearly always a nurse. Potentially either, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Upon your direction, Nurse Lucy Letby agreed to reposition that tube. Your note seems to have an additional entry at 05.26.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "Nasogastric tube re-passed with acidic gastric aspirates by Lucy Letby."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Is that an indicator that, once re-passed, it was in the appropriate position?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy, before we leave the X-ray, under the comments section?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That says:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "Patchy bilateral air space shadowing. Bowel loops distended. No free air. No pneumatosis. No portal air identified."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Could you explain that to us in layman's terms, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It suggests that there's some subtle changes in [Baby I]'s lungs, denoted by the air space shadowing. That's a nonspecification finding, just suggesting the lungs are not -well, it's relatively subjective, but the lungs are not as completely well aerated as they might be otherwise.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: The next two lines relate to an assessment of the bowel gas pattern on an abdominal X-ray. It suggests that [Baby I]'s bowel loops were distended, but that there was no evidence of any air having leaked out of the bowel into the surrounding abdominal tissue, so no free air and no air leaking into the wall of the bowel and no air leaking into the liver system.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we then just consider your plan of action as noted towards the foot of the page?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To repeat her blood gas test in 1 hour, to review the bloods that had been sent for a full blood count, CRP, urea and electrolytes, and bone profile. To review in the morning for possible transfer as discussed with Dr Newby. Hourly blood pressures, monitoring urine output and keeping nil by mouth.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Please focus momentarily upon the contemplation of the possibility of a transfer (inaudible: coughing) transfer to where and why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So to one of the tertiary neonatal centres and because of the period of instability overnight.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. For your Lordship's note, those clinical notes are also behind tiles 95 and 96. The 05.26 hours note is behind tile 96.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Neame. My Lord, the remainder of Dr Neame's evidence is pertinent to the events recorded on a later sequence of events for [Baby I], which will be presented to the jury this morning and his evidence will be better understood if it's given after.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Keeping things in sequence?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Quite so.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: You understand that?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I understand, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you very much. So that's it for the time being. No, sorry, Mr Myers, do you want to ask questions at this stage?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes. I understand it might have been thought that I might deal with that at the conclusion but perhaps I might deal with these points now.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Of course. Whatever you wish to do.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Dr Neame, just going back, on Friday we went to your notes which you made for 5 September. Just to refresh our minds, [Baby I] was born on 7 August. The first event we come to that we're looking at specifically in this trial is on 30 September. We've just been looking at the second event, which is 13 October. I just want to go back to what you were telling us about relating to 5 September, so about a month or so after [Baby I] was born and several weeks before we come to the first event that we are focusing on.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have just said that so we can all zero in on what I'm talking about and what you're going to answer questions about.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I'm going to ask Mr Murphy to put up page 13773.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: It's from your clinical notes, Dr Neame, and we looked at it on Friday. It's something which is additional to the sequence of events, so it'll either come up on the screens or it may in fact be in the additional section under this part of the case, ladies and gentlemen.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Just to re-familiarise with this, these are your notes made at about 9.30 on the morning of 5 September, Dr Neame?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And you're familiar with these, aren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm not going to read through everything we have in them, but I'm going to ask if we could go to the following page, 13774, following them through.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see the notes for that morning carry on halfway down the page.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: You indicated on Friday that in general you had no concerns for [Baby I] at this point; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: We can see there, just towards the end of the note, it says -- what is it that's underlined, by the way, the word there? It says "[something] well baby".
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Impression."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Impression, thank you. Your impression then was that she was a well baby?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So as at about 9.35 on 5 September, she seemed to be a well baby and no particular matters of concern?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Although always with a little neonate like this in her condition, you have to be watchful, don't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: That's at 9.35. If we carry on down that page, we come to your note that starts at 9 o'clock on the same day.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: 21.00 hours.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I want to stick to the 24-hour clock.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I'm grateful. 21.00 hours the same day, so about 12 hours later in fact.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: We can see now that you've attended because of a desaturation that's taken place; is that right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: You make the point that, so far as you understood, she'd been generally well today; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But there's an increasing frequency in desaturations over the last hour?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So this is something which has come about unexpectedly in fact; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Right. The rest of that note continues as you deal with [Baby I]. If we go down to the bottom of the page, please, we can see under the letters OE, which means "on examination", you have put:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Alert, active and pink."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That describes the baby, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But you've also noted "very frequent desaturations" and then what's the word under that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It's "nadir", so lowest --
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: At the lowest point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "... 60% oxygen and also slight bradycardia now."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So slowing of the heart rate?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: That's in the region -- is that about 100?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "No apnoeas at this point"?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: That's what the bottom bit means, doesn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's right.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: We're getting the idea that when it has an O above the word that means no apnoeas?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: I would just like to carry through what happens for the benefit of the jury, Dr Neame. If we go to page 13775.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: We can see the conclusion of your note for 21.00. Then we can see -- if we just scroll down, please, we get into notes now made by Dr Ventress, which start at 22.30 hours.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: We see that. We've had evidence read from Dr Ventress and I'm not going to go through all of these, at this point, but I just want to identify, if we look at the bottom part of that page, we can see after the first few lines, it says:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Twenty minutes after feed at 22.20 had profound desaturation down to 50% sats."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Can you see that, Dr Neame?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, I can.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Then Dr Ventress sets out the action taken to deal with the problems as she dealt with it, and I'd like to go over the page, please to, 13776, just moving forwards.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The next entry is at 01.00. It says 5 September 15, but in fact that's 6 September 2015, 01.00.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: If we just enlarge right next to that, please. We can see now that by about 23.15, [Baby I] has another profound desaturation to 50%. Then there's actions taken to deal with that. But you can see where it says "Profound desaturation to 50%", Dr Neame?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: The decision was taken, this is just to keep us apace with what's happening, to intubate [Baby I] at this point.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would like to move next, please, to page 13778 and the lower entry there, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So we are going through the evening with Dr Ventress dealing with [Baby I] and we can see now, 6 September 2015, 03.40 in the morning, Dr Ventress was crash called to the neonatal unit at 03.26 because [Baby I] had a profound desaturation on the
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: ventilator and started to drop her heart rate. Do you see that, Dr Neame?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Then just to complete what happens, in summary, the problems continued with [Baby I]'s condition and we know that she was transferred to the Liverpool Women's Hospital at 15.41 on 6 September. That's actually under tile 7 on part 1 of the [Baby I] sequence, but we perhaps don't need to go there, I just identify that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: [Baby I] went to Liverpool Women's Hospital at 15.41 on 6 September.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I identify all that, Dr Neame, because, I'm not taking issue with you, but as of 9 o'clock on 5 September, she had appeared to be a well baby with no impending problems that you could identify; that's correct, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But she deteriorated significantly overnight, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She did, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And that meant that the following day, by 3 o'clock, a little after 15.00 hours in the afternoon, she'd had to be transferred to Liverpool Women's Hospital, which is a tertiary centre, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So that's the 5th and 6 September.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I'd just like to move forward to what you have been telling us now about 13 October, Dr Neame, a couple of points about that. We can move forwards now to event 2.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Event 1 was 30 September.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: On 13 October, when you went to the unit -- we've just been dealing with this now -- in response to the call, was [Baby I] receiving Neopuff ventilation at that point?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, that's my recollection.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Right. I don't want you to be at any disadvantage. I'm going to ask Mr Murphy now just to put up the tile 49 we were looking at in case you want to refer to it.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No, I mean her weight was low and obviously, as we've seen, it had dropped down the centiles, but she had had numerous episodes throughout her life where we had been unable to feed her because of abdominal distension or initially when she was first born and she was ventilated. blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Right. So following on from that point, when we looked at your notes earlier this morning and you described [Baby I] as stable as a consequence of those notes, was that a feature that you had in mind when you considered her to be a stable baby?

blocks.text: Mm-hm.

blocks.text: It was, yes.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Babies are usually proportionate for weight, for length, for head circumference and often if -- so birth weight is very much to do with maternal health and placental health rather than the baby itself, really. So a baby that has a good birth weight, mum's had a healthy placenta, the head circumference will often be in proportion to the birth weight. If the placenta has not been healthy, then you might find a baby with a larger head circumference centile than a weight centile because nature always spares the brain.
blocks.speaker: NEWBY

blocks.text: Favours the brain?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Favours the brain, yes.

blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I currently work in the accident and emergency department of Arrowe Park Hospital. I have been asked about my recollections and knowledge of a baby called [Baby I], who required resuscitation in the early hours of 13 October 2015 at the Countess of Chester Hospital.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "In 2015 I was training to become a GP. My training included rotating between different departments for a period of 4 months at a time. blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I can't assist with anything further, I'm afraid. I don't remember which nurses were present during the resuscitation or which room [Baby I] was in at the time. I can't remember the names of doctors or nurses who worked on the unit at the time."

blocks.text: That concludes her statement.

blocks.text: Witness statement of MS LAURA EAGLES (read)
Moving on, my Lord, to Laura Eagles, please, and a statement dated 24 October 2018. She describes herself as a senior neonatal nurse and says as follows:
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been spoken to about my recollections of and involvement with a baby called [Baby I] while she was on the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester during 2015.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I was asked about 12 October into 13 October 2015. I was on a night shift on that date. Prior to providing this statement, I have had the opportunity to review the nursing notes.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "From those notes and my own recollections, [Baby I] was in special care and was in a cot. She was on four-hourly feeds. She had been very sick off and on, but at that time she was having no interventions other than having her temperature monitored as she was well.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "She always had a big tummy and we always had to note how distended her abdomen was, whether it was bigger or smaller. That was her main concern. She was at that point still on cefotaxime. She had been treated for an infection 6 days prior. I wasn't looking after her on that night, it was Ashleigh Hudson. Caroline Oakley was in charge. I'm only noted in the notes as coming to assist but I didn't make any notes myself.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Lucy Letby was on duty that night, as was Janet Cox, who is a nursery nurse. I have read what happened. I don't remember the exact chronological order of what happened, but I do remember [Baby I]'s collapse that night.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I'm sure she was in nursery 2. She may have been further along, but I don't think so. She'd been found pale and with shallow breathing. I was called to assist and I seem to remember pulling the cot into the middle of the room so we had more access to her.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Dr Clegg was the SHO, but I don't know if she was on the unit already and we just shouted her, or whether she was bleeped. We started Neopuffing her [Baby I] and putting her on a monitor because she wasn't on a monitor and started chest compressions as her heart rate was less than 60 beats per minute, so that was normal practice.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The registrar was Dr Neame and he was bleeped and came back and took over the airway, which left the nurses free to get drugs
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: and equipment out. I remember us resuscitating her and Dr Newby also being there, but I don't know at what point she was phoned or by whom.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "We moved [Baby I] into nursery 1 once we had stabilised her airway. You can't move babies until you are happy with their airway. Once we had stopped the compressions it was just a quick wheel a few metres round the corner through to nursery 1 to put her on the ventilator. So I do remember most of that not just from reading it.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I think the notes say that Dr Neame took the airway control off Lucy. I am not sure if I was doing chest compressions, but it's more likely the SHO was doing that and I was getting the resus trolley and getting the drugs out. The resus trolley is kept on nursery 1. You rip the tag off it to open it and take the drugs out.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I have been told that Ashleigh Hudson recalls going into nursery 1 to assist me with a cannula that night, which is why she was away from [Baby I]. I can't recall that, although it wouldn't be unusual for me to ask for assistance doing that. I have been told it was for a septic screen, but I don't have a personal recollection of that."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: My Lord, that concludes what she says about that particular event.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "My next entry was on 12 October at 11.15 hours in the morning. At this point we were just finishing off the antibiotics and we'd given her a blood transfusion. Between this date and my previous entry (inaudible: distorted) which was not uncommon. They [meaning babies] will slowly get anaemic over time and will require blood transfusions and I have written 'anaemia of
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: prematurity'. We were now just monitoring her bloods as her blood count was quite low. She was feeding well and handling well and pink with a capillary refill less than 2, heart sounds were fine, tummy was soft, and she had bowel sounds.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Her CRP had gone from 71 to 21 and now down to 8, so that was really good. There were no concerns at that point.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I wasn't on duty that night, but I am aware that at 03.36 on 13 October, [Baby I] was found by a nurse to be pale, lifeless and gasping for air. blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "The next entry I made on the notes was later in the day, on 13 October at 16.00 hours. I had gone to review her at that point in time because of how poorly she'd been earlier. I wrote that her blood gases and her ventilation were all acceptable. Her blood pressure had been dropping throughout the day. She'd been put on dopamine, which had improved it. blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "I had also inserted a long line at that time into her right thigh. I do remember that she was quite a tricky one when it came to lines and the thigh was quite an unusual place to put one. You tend to put them in the ankles.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "At that stage we were waiting to hear back from the surgeons to find out what they thought, but otherwise I would describe her as sick but stable and still on the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: "With regards to her earlier collapse, we were thinking along the lines of NEC. In that time her abdomen had got larger and firmer, so that was our running thought. She had never got as far as surgery and I think her parents were quite upset at the fact she had never been seen by the surgeons and not a lot was happening, but to be honest there was never anything on the Xrays or that had been massively convincing that she required surgery. There was nothing definitive in relation to NEC, but it was grumbling on."
blocks.speaker: MR ASTBURY

blocks.text: That her abdomen was uncomfortable and tender at that point.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. You haven't put it on the note, but can you expand upon the mottling or not from memory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I... I don't recall it clearly, but it is unusual to see and to have recorded abdominal mottling specifically.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So did you seek to address the problem by increasing the Neopuff pressure?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I increased the pressure, noted that there was some improvement in the movement of her chest wall and noted an improvement in her oxygen saturation level with that change, therefore I restarted the ventilator, the automatic breathing machine, with some increased pressures and an increased concentration of oxygen.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you then express an opinion or, in your terminology, state your impression?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So my impression was that the increasing abdominal distension may have caused [Baby I]'s lungs to become squashed, essentially, making it harder for her to breathe, maintain normal oxygen levels. That was my impression.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you expand upon that process for us, the relationship between a distended tummy and impaired breathing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So normal breathing, respiration, requires muscles in the chest wall and in the diaphragm, the big muscle at the bottom of the lungs, to move up and down. If they are -- particularly if the diaphragm is unable to move down, that can limit expansion of the chest wall and can limit the effectiveness of breathing.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Your plan as formulated at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: In addition to increasing the pressures on the ventilator, to repeat -- well, to obtain chest and abdominal Xrays urgently, to do the planned bloods sooner, repeat a blood gas test, and to increase the dose of morphine to make [Baby I] more comfortable.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So going back to the beginning of this entry, you were asked to review the patient. Can you remember by whom or in what circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't remember the circumstances particularly.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: I think it was by Lucy Letby.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. In summary, how did [Baby I] present at this point in time as compared to your night review at 22.05 on 13 October?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So she was more unwell, as evidenced by the low oxygen levels and the need for increased breathing support at that point. And the other aspect that stands out from my memory and from the notes is the change in the appearance of her abdomen with the change in the skin and the increased tenderness.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Can you remember how you received the request to attend upon the baby, the method of communication?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't remember, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Can you remember your interaction with the nurse upon attending, your initial interaction?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't think I can, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you very much. Could we then, please, Mr Murphy, go to tile 90?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a note written by you at 08.10, but it refers to discussions with Dr Jayaram at an earlier point in time. Does it follow that you felt the need to speak to your on-call consultant Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. I spoke to him having arranged the X-rays and the blood gas tests, is my memory.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And was in general terms the subject matter of that discussion the readings and the examination that we've just seen your notes for?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, with the results of the X-rays as well.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: With the additional information of the X-ray results?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: What was the nature and the consequence, if any, of the discussion with the on-call consultant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To discuss the findings from the abdominal X-ray, which included some dilation of the loops of bowel, noted the smaller than expected appearance of [Baby I]'s lungs, and an area of collapse in the right upper zone of [Baby I]'s right lung.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Did that tend to inform your view as to whether the relationship between the distended tummy and the impaired breathing was as you feared a little earlier?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, those findings were in keeping with that assessment.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So you had -- on the basis of your clinical observations you formed that suspicion and on reviewing an X-ray they were confirmed?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I think the right upper lobe -- so the changes in [Baby I]'s right upper lung are perhaps not related to that but the small appearance of the lungs and the dilated appearance of the bowel loops would be, if that makes sense. So I think the changes in the right upper lung might be different.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: I understand. Different and related to it or different and independent to it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Possibly related to being managed on the ventilator or complications of having been unwell from the previous 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you summarise the advice or guidance you received from Dr Jayaram?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To continue with the ventilation settings that [Baby I] was receiving, to check again for evidence of a pneumothorax, and to discuss those factors with the surgical team at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you have such a discussion with Alder Hey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I did.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Have you recorded it here?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Mr Lamont?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: His registrar, the on-call registrar who was working with Mr Lamont, who was one of the consultants at that time.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Yes. What advice did you get and how did you act on that advice if at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So they advised that they would look at [Baby I]'s X-rays and contact us with a plan following discussion in the morning with Mr Lamont, the consultant.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. When you communicated with Alder Hey, I'll just use the hospital term, I'm not sure the identity of the person -- was that by telephone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: By phone, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And where would that conversation have taken place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Somewhere on the neonatal unit, I can't remember where.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Would it have been via landline or mobile phone?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Landline.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. I think omitted the preface to this, apologies: was a cold light test performed at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall doing it, but I think I recall in the notes that it was negative.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy, if we see a little further -- the other direction, please. There we go. Does that record there was a cold light test?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, negative cold light examination.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. The next entry, we can look at it here, but I think it is reproduced on our visual display behind tile 104. Again, if we just look at this for context -- go firstly to tile 102, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We see what's been recorded as an event between two entries, both of which were recorded at 07.00. Then we go to tile 104. Thank you. We can look at Dr Neame's notes behind there.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Written in retrospect at 08.10. We've just seen this reference to your communication with Dr Jayaram.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we go down until we see at 07.00, thank you, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Can you tell us, Dr Neame, what happened with [Baby I] at that point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: [Baby I] had a significant desaturation with a bradycardia, low heart rate, not improving with management using the Neopuff machine. Therefore a decision was made to replace [Baby I]'s breathing tube to exclude an airway issue as the cause of that episode.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Could you expand, please, upon what airway issue was in your mind at that point in time that caused you to decide to replace the tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It could be a problem with a misplacement of the tube or it becoming dislodged or it could be a problem with the tube itself becoming blocked with secretions.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Was the quickest and the most expedient way of addressing that simply to remove it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I think with a period like this, it's important to exclude that as a factor in the presentation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So it was removed. Did you replace it with a different sized tube or the same sized tube?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall whether it was a 3.5 or 3-millimetre tube that [Baby I] had.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Originally?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Originally, yes. But a similar sized tube and then secured and tested in the usual way.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: By which you mean you satisfied yourself that it was 8 centimetres at the lips?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and then I checked that there was equal air entry, listening to [Baby I]'s chest, used the capnography tool as well, and requested an X-ray to check the positioning of the tube. Those changes seemed to improve [Baby I]'s saturation levels alongside, again, a further increase in the pressures used on the Neopuff machine, and those resulted in [Baby I]'s oxygen saturations improving to 100%, so she was placed back on the ventilator again with some increased pressures and an oxygen level of 100% on the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So did you note an improvement in her saturation levels before you adjusted the ventilation settings or after?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall at the time. I think it refers to a general improvement following the change of tube and the adjustment in her ventilation settings.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. If we look at the remainder of this note, Mr Murphy. Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So having noted an improvement, what happened next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Unfortunately, there was a further episode of desaturation with low oxygen levels, this time despite good air entry, good chest wall movement and a negative cold light test. Because of that further episode I called for Dr Jayaram to come to the hospital.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you please explain the use of the word "despite" in that sentence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So despite confirmation that the breathing tube seemed to be working well, with a good effect on [Baby I]'s chest wall movement, the desaturation seemed to occur despite using the clinical tools we have to rule out a problem with the ventilation system at that time.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And despite a negative cold light test?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thus ruling out --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: As best as we can a pneumothorax.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: An air leak?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Then further desaturation, despite using the Neopuff machine and despite generous/good pressures on the Neopuff machine at that point, and even with those interventions, [Baby I] became bradycardic so her heart rate dropped and her oxygen levels dropped to 60%. So then I made a plan to administer muscle relaxant medicine and to give [Baby I] some extra fluid to try and improve her circulation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: What was the purpose of administering the muscle relaxant substance?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Due to ongoing concerns about pressure from the abdomen impeding ventilation, a muscle relaxant can help with that process, reduce resistance to ventilation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we go to tile 117, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mr Driver, we're going to have to have a break at some time. I don't know whether that's a convenient point.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It is, thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: It is 3 o'clock now.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think we've got quite a lot of work to do this afternoon because the next witness will have difficulty being here tomorrow, so can we make it a five-minute break, please? If you want longer, you may have longer, but if you are ready to come back in 5 minutes, that would be helpful.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the absence of the jury)

My Lord, just to assist with the timing, it occurs to me just to say this: Dr Jayaram's statement was prepared relatively recently, not making any criticism about that, and he wasn't a witness we had anticipated to deal with. He's not a witness we anticipate having cross-examination for unless the evidence takes a particular turn. I just say that to assist. Depending on how his evidence is, there may be none or little
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: cross-examination in his case.
All right, thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: We won't know until we get there.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Exactly. I don't know how much longer this --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: I think we're on schedule to finish at the customary time.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Good, all right. We'll see how we get on.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much. We've used up 2 minutes of the 5 minutes, but if anyone wants to have a break, I'll rise just for 3 minutes and I'll be back.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (A short break)

Dr Neame, we're in the morning of Wednesday, 14 October. We've just considered entries that you made in relation to events at 7 am, at 7.10 am, and now we are about to look at notes that you made at 08.10 in relation to matters a little earlier.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Please, Mr Murphy, I'm grateful.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So we go down to, I think, 07.45. What happened at 07.45, Dr Neame?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: At 7.45 [Baby I]'s heart rate went below 60 beats per minute, therefore chest compressions, cardiopulmonary resuscitation was initiated. [Baby I] was administered a bolus of saline fluid. Her chest wall was checked with a cold light to again rule out an air leak, a pneumothorax. She had another dose of a muscle relaxant. At that time the capnography, carbon dioxide test, was positive and she had chest wall movements and equal air entry listening to her chest.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Together, what did those pieces of information tell you, positive capnography and equal chest movement?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: They suggested that [Baby I] had a stable airway.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So the tube was in the right place?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. You told us that you undertook a cold light test. What was the result?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was negative. So no air leak detected.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Yet her heart rate had fallen below 60?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Which is how low?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, it's low, dangerously low, and that's why we used chest compressions at that point.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. If we look down at the remainder of your note, please. CPR was ongoing and adrenaline was used at 07.48, why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's part of the resuscitation process when there's concerns about the baby's heart rate being too low.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Sodium bicarbonate was given. Again, is that part of the same protocol?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Part of the resuscitation protocol, yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: For your Lordship's note, that event is recorded behind tile 118. We'll stay with this page, but behind tiles 120 and 121, did you have cause to give [Baby I] a second dose of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at 07.53.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Is that because the first dose had not succeeded in raising the heart rate to a level that you thought was safe?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Was there then a requirement for a further dose of adrenaline?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at 07.56.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Did that have the desired effect?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, at 07.58 [Baby I] had a spontaneous heart rate, which would have been over 60 at that point.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So in short, were the circumstances such that urgent CPR was required with the resuscitation protocol adopted, but on this occasion it proved successful?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Dr Jayaram will give evidence shortly, but did he join you and did you effectively hand over principal responsibility to Dr Jayaram at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we move forward in time, please, Mr Murphy, and go to tile 248, which, as we can all see, takes us to 21.30 hours on 14 October.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we have just left the morning and we are now well into the night of the same date. Were you called again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, asked to see [Baby I] regarding a period of desaturation, low oxygen levels.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Did you note that by the time you arrived, she had recovered?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, and that she was placed back on the ventilator and with the ventilator settings recorded there as well.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Are they exceptional recorded levels of ventilation or are they normal for the circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, they're certainly much better than they were over the night before, so she wasn't needing as much pressure or as much supplemental oxygen at that point.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So reduced pressure, reduced supplemental oxygen, and her saturation levels were at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: There was a breathing tube in and did all indicators suggest that those were in the right place and, working well?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: You then reviewed some gas, blood gas readings, that had been taken 2.5 hours earlier or thereabouts --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, a good gas.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- 19.00 hours? You recorded them as being good?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Would that reflect the sort of readings that you explained to us a little earlier in your evidence this afternoon?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. You then comment that there was some movement in her legs. What's the significance of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't recall the timeline precisely at this moment, but I think it may have been that [Baby I] was having some medicine to give her some muscle paralysis at that time.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So it's a way of measuring the dose of that.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So if so, perhaps she was not receiving sufficient, is that the purpose of that or was that (overspeaking) reaction?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's a way of gauging how much or how much an effect it was having.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Keep going down the page, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was there a problem with the line, that being an intravenous line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "The line has been occluding but now infusing freely."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And then --
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Decode that for us.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the pumps that help to infuse fluids and medicines through the lines that we use have pressure sensors on them. If the pressure is too high because the line is occluded or kinked for any reason they'll stop pumping.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So from that note, the line had been doing that or the pumps had been alarming, suggesting an occlusion, but at that point they were working well and the medicines and fluids were infusing freely.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you move the line at that point? Did you reposition the line? Look at the plan.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It said "line repositioned". I don't know if that was someone had done it and the team were happier with the functioning of the line or whether it was me that did it. I don't recall, I'm afraid.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you take us through the remainder of your plan?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So it says [Baby I] was more active, then increased morphine back to the previous rate that was a bit higher and consider muscle relaxant medicines. If any increased ventilation requirements, again to consider using muscle relaxant/paralysing medicines and increasing sedation for [Baby I].
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. So to summarise that, at this point in time her respiration was sound, this was precautionary advice should she deteriorate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we please go to tile 278. Now we've moved into 15 October, I think. That would appear to be the entry at 21.30 -- down the bottom, there it is, thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you explain or expand upon the entries first at 23.00 and then at 00.40, the following morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the 23.00 entry says:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "More active, breathing against vent. Tidal volumes decreasing down to 3-4ml per kilogram."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. "Breathing against vent"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So if the ventilator's giving scheduled breathing support, if a baby's more active and is breathing in a way
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: that's asynchronous or out of time with the ventilator, that can cause problems, if essentially the baby is trying to breathe out as the ventilator is trying to breathe in, that can be uncomfortable and can impact the ventilation support that you're trying to administer.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So was the plan to sedate her further so as to allow the breathing apparatus to do the work for her?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. And to repeat blood gas testing --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: -- in due course. Then at 00.40 on 15 October?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It says:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "Cannula reinserted into left foot. Can give blood over 3 hours due to delay incurred whilst obtaining IV access."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So I think that refers to -- well, the insertion of a cannula and then whereas often we'd give blood over 4 hours, if the blood had been waiting to be administered it would be -- my note recommends giving the blood over a slightly shorter time to make sure that the correct dose is given.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy, tile 292, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So further into the morning of 15th, we're now at 02.00 hours. Did you examine [Baby I] again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So I've noted [Baby I] continues to breathe regularly, that her tidal volumes are very variable, between 2 and 5ml per kilogram, that [Baby I]'s blood gas is less good, a borderline gas, on her ventilator settings. So her pH, blood acidity, has reduced a bit, suggesting her blood's becoming more acidic, her carbon dioxide is higher than normal, but her other markers in the blood gas are normal at that point.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: So does that indicate a deterioration in the quality of her breathing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. The ventilation that we're providing is not working as effectively as it had been.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And so your plan was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Another slightly smaller dose of the muscle relaxant and to increase the -- just on the line that's coming out of the screen -- to increase the rate --
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Mr Murphy, could you -- thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To increase the rate on the ventilator to 45 and the pressure to increase that to 22 from, I think, 20/5, with a repeat blood gas an hour following those changes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Is the next entry yours?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I think that's Dr Saladi's.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Could we please go, Mr Murphy, to, I think, tile 299.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It is a note of yours at 04.00 hours. Were you called to see [Baby I] again?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: And why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I was called to see her due to low oxygen levels that weren't improving using the Neopuff machine and not improving using increasing pressures on the Neopuffing machine. At that time the capnography test was negative, suggesting that the tube was either dislodged or blocked, so I removed the breathing tube.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. And upon removal, how did she respond, if at all?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She improved well using the Neopuff machine with her oxygen levels returning to 100%.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Keep looking further down the page, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You then removed that tube. Can you remember why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I think... Could we scroll up?
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Please, a few lines.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Then I replaced the tube. The carbon dioxide test, the capnography, was negative and her air entry was poor, therefore the tube was removed.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. How did that go, the removal and attempted re-intubation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The procedures at the time went smoothly, but the checks that we do to check that the tube is working effectively were concerning again, so again the capnography was negative and the breathing checks were also concerning as well, so...
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Thank you. Why would that be so if it seemed to you that the procedure had gone well?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, there's the possibility that even though you've seen the tube go through the cords, that it's become dislodged, possibly when removing the instrument that we use to visualise those cords. I mean, in this case I go on to perform another manoeuvre where I've used extra suctioning further down between [Baby I]'s vocal cords and that seemed to improve the situation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Could you expand on that for us?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Another similar attempt to improve the situation by replacing the breathing tube was unsuccessful with a slightly smaller tube there, so that's the:
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: "3-millimetre ETT passed, again good visualisation of the cords and tube seen passing through the cords."
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: But again the carbon dioxide test remained negative.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: At that point we tried suctioning through the breathing tube itself to see if that would improve the situation.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: Then the note's just running out there.
blocks.speaker: NEAME

blocks.text: I think one of the things you advised him was to exclude a pneumothorax?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes. So you may remember from a previous testimony, I discussed in this situation when a child becomes acutely unwell there's a concept of the 4Hs and the 4Ts.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We have to think what's caused this. Is it due to hypoxia? So is the primary problem lack of oxygen. Is it hypovolaemia, so is there not enough fluid in the circulation. Is it hypothermia? And there wasn't an issue with temperature. Is it related to low sugars or any electrolyte imbalances, which there didn't seem to be, and there's the Ts as well.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So in this situation, thinking through, knowing that there had been a respiratory deterioration in association with a distended abdomen, the thinking was: is the distended abdomen actually contributing to the difficulties in ventilation? And that can happen for a number of reasons. The first reason is mechanical.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If the abdomen is very distended it pushes upwards on the diaphragm. The diaphragm is the muscle that separates everything in the chest from the abdomen and in breathing, the diaphragm goes up and down. If the abdomen is very distended it's harder for the diaphragm to move and it can compress the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: When an abdomen is distended, it also pushes on the inferior vena cava, which is the main blood vessel that carries blood back to the heart and it can reduce the amount of blood that gets carried back to the heart, which in turn has an effect on the heart's ability to pump blood around the body.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: We also had to think, is there a lung problem as well? And in a ventilated baby acutely -- with an acute deterioration, a pneumothorax also has to be considered.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So at that time I felt it was important, before thinking about anything else, to exclude a pneumothorax, which can be done with a cold light, but also in view of this unexplained unusual abdominal distension, to speak with the surgical team at Alder Hey.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Okay. I think that's also on his note. And before we leave the note, if we go to the second substantial paragraph, Dr Neame carried out the cold light test:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: replacement, things seemed to improve, although [Baby I] was needing quite high-pressure ventilation in order to get the lungs to move. We can see there it says 35/5. The bottom number 5 is the background pressure, the PEEP, which helps to splint the lungs open, and the top pressure is the pressure given with each breath. That's higher than it had been and it is quite a high pressure, which suggests that the lungs -- it was difficult to inflate the lungs.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: If we look at the last paragraph that we can see on Dr Neame's note, despite, is this right, changing the tube, [Baby I] desaturated again despite the record being:
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: "Good air entry, chest wall movement and negative cold light"?

blocks.text: Do you see that entry?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, absolutely.

blocks.text: So on the face of it, the ETT is doing its job, air going in and out --
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: -- carbon dioxide importantly coming out but still desaturating?
blocks.speaker: ASTBURY

blocks.text: Yes, and at that point we hadn't done a blood gas but the fact that the baby is desaturating and not able to oxygenate at this point is of concern. That would suggest that the degree of abdominal distension, knowing that the tube is in the right place, knowing that there's no evidence of a pneumothorax, the degree of abdominal distension is probably causing such compression to the lungs that even though we could see the chest moving and gas was going in and out, there was probably an issue being caused with blood flowing through the lungs as well. So it's a combination of things here, really, in retrospect. We've got massive abdominal distension, we've got a situation where we know the tube is in, and Matthew has documented that the chest wall is moving, so gas is going in and out of the lungs, but in spite of this, in 100% oxygen, we can't get good saturations.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And what happens usually in that situation is that because the lungs are so stiff, the resistance to blood flow through the lungs increases because the lungs are stiff and then you get into a vicious circle because the oxygen levels being low mean that the lungs get stiffer.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: I'll try and explain it as simply as I can. As I mentioned, the PEEP is the lower number on the ventilator setting, which was 5 centimetres, which is fairly standard for a baby of [Baby I]'s gestation. PEEP helps to keep the lungs open. So at the end of a breath out, at the end of an expiration, there's a tendency for the alveoli, the air sacs, to collapse down and it helps to keep them open. If you don't have PEEP on, effectively you are obstructing the airway with your endotracheal tube and the airways are more likely to collapse down. So PEEP is important.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: PEEP in itself can cause trouble because if your PEEP is too high it can cause retention of carbon dioxide. If you like, you're blowing so hard into the lungs it's actually hard to breathe out again.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: And the other problem with PEEP is that it can increase the pressure in the whole of the thorax, in the whole of the chest.

blocks.text: We had a situation here where we knew, because of the fact that the abdomen was distended and was pushing on the diaphragms, that we had a number of conflicting things to think about. We obviously had to try to ventilate better in order to get rid of carbon dioxide.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: But we also needed to give enough PEEP to stop the lungs from collapsing down. And we had a situation where the lungs were already compressed anyway.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: Now the rationale for decreasing PEEP is that the gap between the peak pressure, that you give a breath, and the PEEP is what's called the tidal volume. And if you increase the tidal volume you blow off more carbon dioxide. So if you -- you're basically making the baby take deeper breaths, effectively, and if you reduce the tidal volume, you may increase the carbon dioxide --
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So another potential advantage of decreasing the PEEP, it would decrease slightly the intrathoracic pressure. blocks.text: We also discussed over the phone increasing the dobutamine. So dobutamine is an infusion of a medication that is designed to help to improve blood pressure. It does that by improving myocardial contractility, so how strongly the heart can contract.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: It can sometimes have an effect the other way by making the peripheral blood vessels dilate a bit more, so you could potentially offset the increase in your myocardial contractility by reducing the blood pressure by making the peripheral vessels dilate. But in this situation we knew that we had stiff lungs. And in order to try and get blood from the right side of the heart to flow to the lungs to pick up oxygen to go back to the left side of the heart to go round the body, we had to try and make sure that the resistance to blood flow in the lungs, so the pulmonary resistance or pulmonary blood pressure was lower than the systemic blood pressure because if the pulmonary blood pressure is higher than your body's blood pressure, blood will preferentially go through the holes in the heart and a thing called the ductus and bypass the lungs. I suspect that's what was happening in a situation where in 100% oxygen we couldn't achieve saturations.
blocks.speaker: JAYARAM

blocks.text: So the rationale for increasing the dobutamine was really, in the context of these lungs being hard to ventilate and resistance to blood flow in them, to try to get a way of getting the systemic blood pressure high enough that blood would preferentially flow through the lungs and therefore pick up the oxygen that was going into the lungs, go back into the heart, and then oxygenated blood would pump around the body.
